📋 Scenario Instructions (Objective 2.5)

You are a field service technician setting up a new SOHO wireless router for a small accounting firm. To comply with security best practices, you must configure the router's web administration GUI according to the following requirements:

  • Network Name (SSID): Set to CorpSecure and keep SSID broadcast enabled.
  • Wireless Security: Enforce the strongest available encryption standard: WPA3-Personal.
  • Passphrase: Set the pre-shared key to Accounting2026!.
  • 2.4 GHz Wireless Channel: Select an industry-standard non-overlapping channel (Channel 1, 6, or 11) with standard 20 MHz channel width.
  • Wi-Fi Protected Setup (WPS): Must be Disabled to prevent brute-force PIN attacks.
  • DHCP IP Pool: Configure start address to 192.168.1.100 and end address to 192.168.1.150.
  • Admin Security: Change the default router management password from admin to AdminRoute#99.

📋 Scenario Instructions (Objective 5.5)

A corporate office has reported four distinct print quality defects occurring on their laser printers. Match each visual defect symptom to its root cause component according to the 7-step laser printing process:

Defect Symptom 1
👻 Ghosting / Duplicate Faint Image

A faint, repeated shadow of the image from earlier on the page appears further down every 3 inches.

Defect Symptom 2
🖐️ Toner Smearing / Rubs Off on Touch

The printout looks crisp coming out, but the toner easily rubs off onto your fingers and smears across the paper.

Defect Symptom 3
📏 Continuous Vertical Black Line

A thin, sharp, continuous black line runs vertically from the very top to the bottom edge of every page printed.

Defect Symptom 4
🌫️ Extremely Faint / Washed-Out Printing

The entire page prints evenly but is extremely light, washed out, and barely legible across all text and graphics.

⚡ Quick Jump Sections

🔌 1. Network Ports & Protocols

Domain 2.0 Networking

Master table of official TCP/UDP port assignments tested on the CompTIA 220-1201 exam.

Port # Protocol Name Transport Default Security Purpose & Exam Distinction
20 / 21 FTP (File Transfer Protocol) TCP Plaintext Port 20 = Data transfer, Port 21 = Control & commands. Sends credentials in cleartext.
22 SSH / SFTP TCP Encrypted Secure Shell remote CLI terminal & SFTP encrypted file transfer over SSH. Replaces Telnet and FTP.
23 Telnet TCP Insecure Unencrypted remote terminal emulation. Sends all keystrokes and passwords in plaintext. Replaced by SSH.
25 SMTP (Simple Mail Transfer) TCP Plaintext Sends outgoing email between mail servers and from client to mail server. Unencrypted by default.
53 DNS (Domain Name System) UDP / TCP Standard Resolves FQDN hostnames to IP addresses. Standard queries use UDP 53; Zone transfers & large payloads use TCP 53.
67 / 68 DHCP / BOOTP UDP Standard Dynamic IP assignment via DORA. Port 67 = DHCP Server, Port 68 = DHCP Client.
69 TFTP (Trivial FTP) UDP No Auth Lightweight UDP file transfer with no user authentication or directory browsing. Used in PXE network boot & router configs.
80 HTTP TCP Plaintext Unencrypted World Wide Web hypertext transfer. Cleartext traffic vulnerable to eavesdropping.
88 Kerberos TCP / UDP Encrypted Authentication protocol used in Windows Active Directory domains. Issues Ticket Granting Tickets (TGT).
110 POP3 (Post Office Protocol 3) TCP Plaintext Downloads incoming email to local client and deletes from server by default. Single-device access model.
123 NTP (Network Time Protocol) UDP Standard Synchronizes clock time across network devices and Active Directory domain controllers to UTC.
137-139 NetBIOS / NetBT UDP / TCP Plaintext Legacy Windows LAN communications: UDP 137 (Name Service), UDP 138 (Datagram), TCP 139 (Session).
143 IMAP4 (Internet Message Access) TCP Plaintext Retrieves incoming email while keeping messages synchronized on the server across multiple devices.
161 / 162 SNMP UDP v1/v2 Plain, v3 Sec Network device monitoring. Port 161 = SNMP Manager queries agent; Port 162 = Agent sends unsolicited Trap alerts. SNMPv3 adds auth & AES encryption.
389 LDAP TCP Plaintext Lightweight Directory Access Protocol. Queries directory services (Active Directory, OpenLDAP) in cleartext.
443 HTTPS TCP TLS/SSL Encrypted web traffic using TLS/SSL cryptographic protocols. Replaces unencrypted HTTP 80.
445 SMB / CIFS TCP Standard Server Message Block. Direct-hosted file and printer sharing in modern Windows networks (bypasses NetBIOS).
465 / 587 SMTPS / Secure SMTP TCP TLS/SSL Encrypted outbound email submission. Port 587 uses STARTTLS (modern standard); Port 465 uses legacy implicit SSL.
548 AFP (Apple Filing Protocol) TCP Proprietary Proprietary Apple macOS local network file sharing protocol.
636 LDAPS (LDAP over SSL) TCP TLS/SSL Encrypted directory service queries using TLS/SSL tunnel. Encrypts Active Directory credentials.
993 IMAPS (IMAP Secure) TCP TLS/SSL Encrypted incoming email retrieval with folder synchronization over TLS/SSL.
995 POP3S (POP3 Secure) TCP TLS/SSL Encrypted incoming email download over TLS/SSL tunnel.
3389 RDP (Remote Desktop) TCP / UDP Encrypted Microsoft proprietary graphical remote desktop administration session.
CompTIA Exam Distractor Traps: Remember plaintext vs. encrypted pairs: HTTP (80) vs. HTTPS (443); Telnet (23) vs. SSH (22); LDAP (389) vs. LDAPS (636); POP3 (110) vs. POP3S (995); IMAP (143) vs. IMAPS (993); SMTP (25) vs. SMTPS (465/587). Also remember: SFTP uses SSH on port 22, whereas FTPS uses FTP over SSL on port 990.

📶 2. Wi-Fi Standards & Frequency Bands

Domain 2.0 Networking

802.11 IEEE wireless standards, frequency bands, speed ceilings, and channel bandwidths.

IEEE Standard Branded Name Frequency Bands Max Theoretical Speed Channel Width Key Technologies & Exam Facts
802.11a Legacy Wi-Fi 1 5 GHz only 54 Mbps 20 MHz Uses OFDM. Short range due to high-frequency absorption by walls; zero 2.4 GHz interference.
802.11b Legacy Wi-Fi 2 2.4 GHz only 11 Mbps 22 MHz Uses DSSS. Longer range than 5 GHz; prone to interference from microwaves, Bluetooth, cordless phones.
802.11g Legacy Wi-Fi 3 2.4 GHz only 54 Mbps 20 MHz Uses OFDM. Fully backward-compatible with 802.11b. Connects at 2.4 GHz speeds.
802.11n Wi-Fi 4 2.4 GHz and/or 5 GHz 600 Mbps (4x4) 20 MHz, 40 MHz Introduced MIMO (Multiple-Input Multiple-Output) and 40 MHz channel bonding. First dual-band standard.
802.11ac Wi-Fi 5 5 GHz only 6.93 Gbps (8x8) 20, 40, 80, 160 MHz Strictly 5 GHz. Introduced Downlink MU-MIMO (Multi-User MIMO), 256-QAM modulation, and beamforming.
802.11ax Wi-Fi 6 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz 9.6 Gbps (8x8) 20, 40, 80, 160 MHz Introduced OFDMA (subdivides channels into resource units), Bi-directional MU-MIMO, 1024-QAM, and Target Wake Time (TWT) for mobile/IoT battery saving.
Wi-Fi 6E Wi-Fi 6 Extended 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, 6 GHz 9.6 Gbps Up to 160 MHz Adds the 6 GHz band (up to 1200 MHz of brand new uncontested spectrum; zero legacy device degradation or microwave interference).
2.4 GHz Channel Rule: In North America (channels 1 to 11), the only three non-overlapping channels are 1, 6, and 11. Each channel is 20 MHz wide with 5 MHz spacing between center frequencies, requiring at least 25 MHz separation to avoid co-channel interference.

📏 3. Cable Types, Speeds & Limits

Domain 3.0 Hardware

Copper twisted pair categories, coaxial ratings, jacket fire codes, and fiber optic transmission limits.

Cable Category Max Bandwidth Frequency Max Certified Distance Standard & Best Use
Cat 3 10 Mbps 16 MHz 100 meters (328 ft) 10BASE-T; legacy analog PBX telephone wiring.
Cat 5 100 Mbps 100 MHz 100 meters (328 ft) 100BASE-TX (Fast Ethernet); deprecated.
Cat 5e 1 Gbps (1000 Mbps) 100 MHz 100 meters (328 ft) 1000BASE-T (Gigabit Ethernet); reduced crosstalk over Cat 5.
Cat 6 1 Gbps / 10 Gbps 250 MHz 100m @ 1 Gbps / 55m @ 10 Gbps 10GBASE-T up to 55 meters; contains internal plastic spline separator.
Cat 6a 10 Gbps 500 MHz 100 meters (328 ft) 10GBASE-T full 100m; augmented shielding eliminates Alien Crosstalk (AXT).
Cat 7 10 Gbps 600 MHz 100 meters (328 ft) Individually shielded pairs (S/FTP); uses GG45/TERA or shielded RJ-45.
Cat 8 25 Gbps / 40 Gbps 2000 MHz 30 meters (98 ft) Data center switch-to-switch top-of-rack interconnects.
🔥 Cable Jacket Fire Ratings
  • CMP (Plenum-Rated): Coated with Teflon (FEP). Emits low smoke and non-toxic fumes. Mandatory for HVAC air return plenum spaces above drop ceilings or below raised floors.
  • CMR (Riser-Rated): Fire-resistant jacket designed for vertical floor-to-floor shafts. Cannot be run through plenum spaces.
  • CM / PVC: Standard patch cables. Emits highly toxic black smoke and corrosive hydrochloric acid gas when burned.
💡 Single-Mode vs Multi-Mode Fiber
  • Single-Mode Fiber (SMF): 9 µm core, yellow jacket. Uses 1310/1550 nm laser light source. Distances: 10 km up to 40+ km. Zero modal dispersion. Used for WAN and campus backbones.
  • Multi-Mode Fiber (MMF): 50 or 62.5 µm core, orange/aqua jacket. Uses 850/1300 nm LED or VCSEL. Distances: 300m to 500m. Limited by modal dispersion. Used for LAN and data centers.

🖨️ 4. Laser Printing Process (7 Steps in Order)

Domain 3.0 Hardware

Memorize the exact 7-step sequence, electrical charges, and component failure symptoms.

Mnemonic: "Can Poor People Read Clean Clear Text?" → Processing, Charging, Exposing, Developing, Transferring, Fusing, Cleaning
1
Processing (Raster Image Processing)
The printer's Raster Image Processor (RIP) renders the document page by page in printer RAM, translating PostScript or PCL code into a raster bitmap image.
Failure: "Out of Memory" error on printer display → Print job too complex, add printer memory.
2
Charging / Conditioning (-600V to -1000V DC)
The primary corona wire or primary charging roller applies a uniform negative electrical charge (-600V to -1000V DC) across the photosensitive drum (OPC).
Failure: Entire page prints completely solid black → Primary corona wire broken or charging roller unseated.
3
Exposing / Writing (-100V Latent Image)
A spinning polygonal mirror deflects a laser beam across the drum, discharging specific spots where toner should go to approximately -100V DC, creating an invisible electrostatic latent image.
Failure: Totally blank page → Laser shutter failed to open or laser diode burned out.
4
Developing (-600V Toner Transfer)
The developer roller coats toner particles (charged negatively to -600V) from the hopper onto the drum. The toner is electrostatically attracted only to the less negative laser-discharged areas (-100V).
Failure: Faint or light printout → Toner cartridge empty or developer roller worn.
5
Transferring (+600V Paper Charge)
The transfer roller or transfer corona wire applies a strong positive electrical charge (+600V) to the underside of the paper, pulling the negatively charged toner particles off the drum onto the paper.
Failure: Completely blank white page → Transfer roller failed (toner remains on drum).
6
Fusing (~350°F / 180°C Heat & Pressure)
The paper passes between a heated halogen fuser roller (~350°F - 400°F) and a rubber pressure roller, melting the toner's plastic resin and permanently bonding it into the paper fibers.
Failure: Toner rubs or smears off page upon touch → Fuser assembly failed to reach temperature.
7
Cleaning (Rubber Scraper & Erase Lamp)
A rubber wiper blade scrapes residual toner from the drum into a waste reservoir. An erase lamp floods the drum with light to neutralize any remaining electrical charge, preparing it for the next page.
Failure: Ghosting (faint duplicate image from previous page) → Damaged wiper blade or bad erase lamp.

💾 5. RAID Configurations (0, 1, 5, 6, 10)

Domain 3.0 Hardware

Minimum disk counts, fault tolerance, usable capacity calculations, and operational performance tradeoffs.

RAID Level Description Min Disks Usable Capacity Fault Tolerance Key Advantage & Use Case
RAID 0 Disk Striping 2 100% (Sum of all drives) 0 Drives Maximum read/write performance. 1 drive failure results in 100% array data loss. For video scratch drives.
RAID 1 Disk Mirroring 2 50% (Size of 1 drive) 1 Drive Copies data identically across drives. High reliability; expensive (50% capacity overhead). For OS boot drives.
RAID 5 Striping with Distributed Parity 3 (N - 1) × Drive Size 1 Drive Balanced capacity and redundancy. Write penalty for parity calculations. For enterprise file servers and NAS.
RAID 6 Striping with Dual Parity 4 (N - 2) × Drive Size 2 Drives Can survive two concurrent drive failures. Higher write penalty. For massive archive storage with long rebuild times.
RAID 10
(1+0)		 Mirrored Sets in a Striped Array 4 (Even) 50% ((N / 2) × Size) 1 per mirror pair High performance striping with mirroring redundancy. Fast rebuild times without parity overhead. For SQL/DBMS.
Hardware RAID vs. Software RAID: Hardware RAID uses a dedicated PCIe controller card with onboard processor, write-cache RAM, and Battery Backup Unit (BBU). It performs array rebuilds in the background with zero CPU overhead. Software RAID is managed by the host OS (e.g. Windows Storage Spaces / Dynamic Disks) and shares system CPU/RAM resources.

🔌 6. Hardware Connectors & Pins

Domain 3.0 Hardware

Motherboard power connectors, display interfaces, peripheral pin counts, and rail voltages.

Connector Name Pin Count Signal / Rails Form Factor & Usage
ATX 24-Pin (20+4) 24 pins +3.3V, +5V, +12V, -12V, +5VSB Main motherboard power connector. Includes PS_ON (pin 16, green wire) and Power Good (gray wire).
EPS12V / ATX12V 4-pin / 8-pin (4+4) +12V (Yellow), Ground (Black) Dedicated CPU power connector delivering +12V directly to motherboard CPU voltage regulator module (VRM).
PCIe Power 6-pin (75W) / 8-pin (150W) +12V (Yellow), Ground (Black) Auxiliary power for dedicated GPU graphics cards. (Note: Motherboard PCIe slot supplies 75W directly).
SATA Power 15 pins +3.3V, +5V, +12V Flat wafer connector with L-shaped keying for internal SSDs, HDDs, and optical drives.
SATA Data 7 pins Serial differential pairs L-shaped keyed data cable. SATA III delivers up to 6.0 Gbps (approx. 550-600 MB/s real-world).
Molex 4-Pin 4 pins +12V (Yellow), +5V (Red), 2x GND Legacy peripheral power connector for IDE hard drives, optical disc drives, and chassis cooling fans.
VGA (DE-15) 15 pins (3 rows of 5) Analog RGBHV video only Legacy analog display port. Susceptible to signal degradation and ghosting over long cables.
DVI-D Single-Link (18+1) / Dual-Link (24+1) Digital only Flat horizontal ground bar with NO surrounding analog pins. Dual-link supports up to 2560x1600 @ 60Hz.
DVI-I Single-Link (18+5) / Dual-Link (24+5) Digital + Analog integrated Horizontal bar surrounded by 4 analog pins (cross pattern). Can be adapted to VGA with passive adapter.
HDMI (Type A) 19 pins Digital video + multi-channel audio HDMI 2.0 (18 Gbps / 4K 60Hz); HDMI 2.1 (48 Gbps / 8K 60Hz, Dynamic HDR, eARC).
DisplayPort 20 pins Packetized video + audio Includes mechanical locking latch. Supports Multi-Stream Transport (MST) for daisy-chaining displays.

☁️ 7. Cloud Models & Services

Domain 4.0 Virtualization & Cloud

Shared responsibility matrix (SaaS vs PaaS vs IaaS), deployment models, and NIST cloud characteristics.

Cloud Model Managed by Provider Managed by Customer Typical Enterprise Examples
SaaS
(Software as a Service)		 Datacenter, hardware, virtualization, OS, runtime, application software, security patches. User credentials, access controls, customer data. Microsoft 365, Google Workspace, Salesforce, Dropbox, ServiceNow.
PaaS
(Platform as a Service)		 Datacenter, physical hardware, hypervisor, host OS, runtime libraries, platform updates. Application code, database schemas, and application data. AWS Elastic Beanstalk, Heroku, Google App Engine, Microsoft Azure App Services.
IaaS
(Infrastructure as a Service)		 Physical datacenter, electrical power, cooling, physical servers, storage arrays, hypervisor. Guest OS, OS patches, middleware, network firewall rules, software applications. Amazon EC2, Microsoft Azure Virtual Machines, Google Compute Engine (GCE).
🌐 Cloud Deployment Models
  • Public Cloud: Multi-tenant infrastructure owned by cloud vendor (AWS, Azure) shared across public clients over the internet.
  • Private Cloud: Dedicated exclusively to a single organization. Maximum security, isolation, and compliance.
  • Hybrid Cloud: Combines public and private clouds connected by encrypted tunnel (VPN/Direct Connect). Enables cloud bursting.
  • Community Cloud: Shared infrastructure for organizations with common compliance or regulatory needs (e.g. healthcare, law enforcement).
⚙️ NIST Cloud Characteristics
  • On-demand self-service: Instant provisioning without human administrator intervention.
  • Broad network access: Ubiquitous access via standard web protocols and thin/thick clients.
  • Resource pooling: Multi-tenant dynamic physical and virtual resource sharing.
  • Rapid elasticity: Instant automated scale-out and scale-in as workloads vary.
  • Measured service: Granular metered billing based on consumed resources (pay-as-you-go).

🌐 8. High-Frequency Acronyms & IP Rules

Domain 2.0 Networking

RFC 1918 private IPv4 blocks, APIPA behavior, loopback diagnostics, and NAT/PAT operations.

IP Address Category Address Range / Notation Subnet Mask / CIDR Behavior & CompTIA Diagnostic Rules
APIPA / Link-Local (IPv4) 169.254.0.1 – 169.254.255.254 255.255.0.0 (/16) Assigned automatically when client cannot reach a DHCP server. Can communicate locally on same subnet; CANNOT reach internet or default gateway.
Link-Local (IPv6) fe80::/10 Prefix fe80:: Mandatory on all IPv6 interfaces. Used for local segment neighbor discovery protocol (NDP); non-routable.
Loopback (IPv4) 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.0/8) 255.0.0.0 (/8) Tests internal TCP/IP software protocol stack without transmitting data to physical NIC hardware.
Loopback (IPv6) ::1 ::1/128 IPv6 counterpart to 127.0.0.1. Tests local protocol stack.
RFC 1918 Class A 10.0.0.0 – 10.255.255.255 255.0.0.0 (/8) Private non-routable IPv4 block. 16.7 million internal host addresses.
RFC 1918 Class B 172.16.0.0 – 172.31.255.255 255.240.0.0 (/12) Private non-routable IPv4 block. 16 contiguous /16 blocks (~1 million hosts).
RFC 1918 Class C 192.168.0.0 – 192.168.255.255 255.255.0.0 (/16) Private non-routable IPv4 block. 256 contiguous /24 blocks (65,536 hosts).
NAT vs. PAT (Port Address Translation): NAT translates private IP addresses to public routable IP addresses. PAT (NAT Overload) maps thousands of private internal IPs to a single public IP address by tracking unique Layer 4 source port numbers in a state table.

📐 9. Motherboard Form Factors & Dimensions

Domain 3.0 Hardware

Physical dimensions, expansion slot limits, standoffs, and UEFI/BIOS firmware rules.

Form Factor Physical Dimensions (Inches) Dimensions (Metric) Max PCIe Slots Chassis Compatibility & Primary Use
Standard ATX 12.0" × 9.6" 305 mm × 244 mm Up to 7 slots Full-tower and mid-tower cases. Standard desktop/workstation motherboard.
Micro-ATX (mATX) 9.6" × 9.6" (Square) 244 mm × 244 mm Up to 4 slots Fits in both micro-ATX and standard ATX cases (screw standoffs share common positions).
Mini-ITX (mITX) 6.7" × 6.7" (Square) 170 mm × 170 mm 1 slot Small Form Factor (SFF) cubes, home theater PCs (HTPC), thin clients.
🔩 Standoffs & Front Panel Headers
  • Motherboard Standoffs: Brass or metal spacers that elevate the PCB off the metal case tray. Missing or misplaced standoffs cause immediate electrical shorts to chassis ground!
  • Front Panel Header: Connects case buttons to motherboard: Power SW (momentary contact), Reset SW, HDD Activity LED, Power LED (+/- polarity matters for LEDs).
🔋 UEFI / BIOS & CMOS Battery
  • UEFI vs. BIOS: UEFI supports GPT partition scheme (> 2 TB drives), GUI mouse support, and Secure Boot (stops bootkits by validating digital signatures).
  • CMOS Battery (CR2032): 3V coin cell powering RTC clock and NVRAM. Symptom of dying battery: System clock resets to 1/1/1970 or 1/1/2000 on power loss.

🏷️ 10. DNS Record Types

Domain 2.0 Networking

Authoritative DNS resource records, mail routing, reverse pointers, and email authentication standards.

Record Type Full Name Maps / Points To Primary Function & Exam Distinction
A Host Address 32-bit IPv4 address Maps a hostname/FQDN to an IPv4 address (e.g. portal.example.com → 192.0.2.1).
AAAA Quad-A Address 128-bit IPv6 address Maps a hostname/FQDN to an IPv6 address (e.g. portal.example.com → 2001:db8::1).
CNAME Canonical Name Another Domain Name Creates an alias pointing one domain name to another domain name. Can NEVER point directly to an IP address!
MX Mail Exchanger Mail Server FQDN Directs incoming email to authorized mail servers. Includes an integer priority value (lowest number = highest priority).
TXT Text Record Arbitrary text string Stores human/machine-readable text. Critical for email security: SPF (authorized sending IPs), DKIM (public signing keys), and DMARC.
NS Name Server DNS Server FQDN Designates the authoritative name servers responsible for resolving records within the DNS zone.
PTR Pointer Record FQDN from IP Reverse DNS resolution (resolves an IP address back to its hostname). Located in in-addr.arpa reverse zone.
SOA Start of Authority Zone metadata First record in every zone file; identifies primary name server, admin contact email, serial number, and zone transfer timers.
SRV Service Record Host & Port Identifies the hostname and TCP/UDP port number for specific enterprise services (e.g. SIP, Active Directory LDAP).
Email Anti-Spoofing Triad (TXT Records): SPF: Lists IP addresses allowed to send mail for the domain. DKIM: Cryptographic digital signature verifying email was not tampered with in transit. DMARC: Specifies policy action (none, quarantine, reject) when SPF or DKIM fails.

🛠️ 11. CompTIA 6-Step Troubleshooting Methodology

Domain 5.0 Troubleshooting

CompTIA's official standardized sequence for diagnosing hardware, software, and network failures.

1
Identify the problem
• Question the user and identify user changes to computer.
• Inquire about environmental or infrastructure changes.
• Perform backups before making changes!
• Review system and application logs (Windows Event Viewer).
2
Establish a theory of probable cause (question the obvious)
• Question the obvious (loose cables, power switches, mute buttons).
• Consider multiple approaches (Divide-and-conquer, Top-to-bottom OSI, Bottom-to-top OSI).
3
Test the theory to determine cause
• Once theory is confirmed, determine next steps to resolve problem.
• If theory is NOT confirmed, re-establish a new theory or escalate!
4
Establish a plan of action to resolve the problem and implement the solution
• Refer to vendor documentation and internal knowledge base.
• Always consider corporate policies, procedures, and potential impact on business workflow.
5
Verify full system functionality and, if applicable, implement preventive measures
• Have the customer or user verify the issue is resolved.
• Verify no secondary issues were introduced by the repair.
• Implement preventive measures (e.g. user training, surge protectors, automatic backups).
6
Document findings, actions, and outcomes
• Record initial problem description, diagnostic steps, parts replaced, and final resolution.
• Update ticketing system and knowledge base for team reference.
CompTIA Exam Traps on Methodology: 1. What is the FIRST thing you do when approaching a client issue? → Question the user / perform backups!
2. If your tested theory fails, what is the immediate next step? → Establish a new theory or escalate! (Never begin implementing changes without a confirmed theory).
3. What do you do immediately after applying a patch or replacing a component? → Verify full system functionality! (Documentation is always the final step).

⚡ 12. USB Standards, Speeds & Power Delivery

Domain 3.0 Hardware

USB revisions, branding aliases, maximum bandwidths, connector colors, and Power Delivery (PD) limits.

USB Standard Market Name Max Speed Max Cable Length Connector Colors & Power Output
USB 2.0 HighSpeed 480 Mbps 5 meters (16.4 ft) White or Black insert. 5V @ 500 mA (2.5W).
USB 3.0 / 3.1 Gen 1 / 3.2 Gen 1 SuperSpeed 5 Gbps 3 meters (9.8 ft) Blue insert. 5V @ 900 mA (4.5W).
USB 3.1 Gen 2 / 3.2 Gen 2 SuperSpeed+ (10Gbps) 10 Gbps 1 meter (3.3 ft) Teal / Aqua insert (or Type-C). Up to 100W with PD.

USB4 USB4 Gen 3x2 40 Gbps 0.8 meters Dual-channel Type-C. Tunneling for Thunderbolt 3/4 & DP 2.0.
Thunderbolt 3 / 4 Thunderbolt 40 Gbps 0.8m – 2m Type-C with Lightning icon. PCIe 4-lane tunneling, dual 4K/single 8K.
USB-C & USB Power Delivery (USB-PD): Type-C has a 24-pin reversible connector. USB-PD dynamically negotiates voltage (5V, 9V, 15V, 20V) delivering up to 100W (20V @ 5A), and USB-PD EPR (Extended Power Range) delivers up to 240W (48V @ 5A) to power gaming laptops and monitors.

🖥️ 13. Mobile Displays & Screen Hardware

Domain 1.0 Mobile Devices

Display panel types (OLED, IPS, TN), backlight technologies, touch digitizers, and bezel antennas.

Display Technology Viewing Angles Color Accuracy Response Time CompTIA Key Takeaways
TN (Twisted Nematic) Poor (color shifts off-axis) Low / Washed out Fastest (1ms) Cheapest LCD panel; high refresh rate; poor viewing angles.
IPS (In-Plane Switching) Excellent (178°) High / Professional Moderate Superb color reproduction and wide viewing angles; ideal for graphic artists.
VA (Vertical Alignment) Moderate Good (Best Contrast) Moderate Deep black levels and high contrast ratio; prone to ghosting.
OLED / AMOLED Near Perfect Vibrant / True Blacks Instantaneous Self-emissive pixels (no backlight!). Infinite contrast; prone to burn-in; thin.
🔦 Backlights & Inverter Troubleshooting
  • Inverter Board: Converts motherboard DC power (~12V) into high-voltage AC (~1000V) for legacy CCFL fluorescent backlights.
  • Flashlight Test: If a laptop screen is black, shine a flashlight at an angle. If faint desktop icons are visible, the inverter board or CCFL bulb has failed.
  • LED Backlights: Modern standard. Powered directly by low-voltage DC (no inverter board needed).
📱 Digitizer & Bezel Routing
  • Digitizer: Touch-sensitive glass pane laminated over the LCD that translates finger/pen touches into digital coordinates. If glass is shattered but image is crisp, only digitizer needs replacing.
  • Antenna Wires: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and cellular antennas are routed up into the display lid/bezel to maximize line-of-sight elevation and avoid chassis interference.

🎨 14. Copper Cabling Pinouts (T568A vs. T568B & Crossover)

Domain 2.0 Networking

RJ-45 (8P8C) color sequences, pin-to-wire pairings, and straight-through vs. crossover cable construction.

T568A Standard Wire Sequence
1 White / Green
2 Green
3 White / Orange
4 Blue
5 White / Blue
6 Orange
7 White / Brown
8 Brown
T568B Standard Wire Sequence (US Commercial)
1 White / Orange
2 Orange
3 White / Green
4 Blue
5 White / Blue
6 Green
7 White / Brown
8 Brown
Pinout Memory Shortcut: Pins 4 & 5 (Blue pair) and Pins 7 & 8 (Brown pair) are in the exact same positions in both T568A and T568B! Only the Green (pins 1 & 2 in A; 3 & 6 in B) and Orange (pins 3 & 6 in A; 1 & 2 in B) pairs swap places.

Straight-Through: Both ends T568B (or both T568A) → Connects unlike devices (PC to Switch, Switch to Router).
Crossover: One end T568A, other end T568B → Connects like devices directly (PC to PC, Switch to Switch without Auto-MDIX).

💡 15. Fiber Optic Connector Types

Domain 2.0 Networking

Physical fiber connectors (ST, SC, LC, MTRJ) and ferrule polish ratings (UPC vs. APC).

Connector Name Physical Latching Mechanism Form Factor Memory Mnemonic & Exam Distinction
ST (Straight Tip) Round metal bayonet twist-lock (BNC-style) Standard "Set and Twist" or "Stick and Turn". Legacy MMF networks.
SC (Subscriber Connector) Square plastic push-pull click latch Standard "Square Connector" or "Stick and Click". Simplex or duplex clip.
LC (Lucent Connector) Small plastic retaining clip (RJ-45 style) Small Form Factor (SFF) "Little Connector". Half size of SC; standard on modern high-density SFP transceivers.
MTRJ Small duplex shell with alignment guide pins Small Form Factor (SFF) Houses two fibers (TX and RX) within a single RJ-45-sized snap latch. Male/female pins.
Ferrule Polish Types (UPC vs. APC):
• UPC (Ultra Physical Contact): Blue connector boot. Flat polished face. Back reflection: -50 dB. Standard data networks.
• APC (Angled Physical Contact): Green connector boot. 8-degree angled ferrule face. Reflected light deflects into cladding. Back reflection: -60 dB (minimal return loss). Mandatory in GPON, FTTx, and video transmissions.
• CompTIA Warning: NEVER connect green APC into blue UPC! The angle creates an air gap, causing severe attenuation and physically scratching the polished cores.

📑 16. Complete Printer Troubleshooting Matrix

Domain 5.0 Troubleshooting

Diagnostic symptoms, root causes, and field solutions across Laser, Inkjet, Thermal, and Impact printers.

Printer Type Observed Symptom / Defect Probable Root Cause Correct Field Solution
Laser Toner smudges / smears off on fingers Cold or damaged Fuser assembly Replace fuser assembly; verify fuser temperature.
Laser Ghosted faint duplicate image from previous page Worn rubber cleaning wiper blade or bad erase lamp Replace drum cleaning blade / toner cartridge; replace erase lamp.
Laser Repetitive marks / dots spaced evenly down the page Scratched photosensitive drum or gouged fuser roller Measure mark spacing: Distance = π × diameter of drum/roller. Replace damaged part.
Laser Page prints solid pitch black Primary corona wire / charge roller failure Replace or clean primary corona wire/roller (drum received no -600V uniform charge).
Laser Completely blank white page Transfer corona / transfer roller broken, or laser shutter stuck Replace transfer roller; inspect and release laser mechanical shutter.
Laser Paper jams / multiple sheets feeding at once Worn, slick pickup rollers or worn separation pad Clean pickup rollers with isopropyl alcohol; replace paper feed kit and separation pad.
Inkjet Streaks, missing horizontal bands of color Clogged printhead ink nozzles Run printer's built-in automated printhead cleaning cycle.
Inkjet Misaligned colors / fuzzy jagged lines Printhead mechanically out of alignment Execute printhead calibration alignment utility from printer menu.
Thermal Blank white paper feeds out with no text Thermal receipt paper roll installed backwards Flip roll over (thermal chemical coating is only on one side; scratch with fingernail to test).
Thermal Faded or very light printout Dirty thermal printhead or low temperature setting Clean printhead with 99% isopropyl alcohol pen; increase print density in settings.
Thermal Sharp white continuous vertical void line through text Burned-out heating element pin on thermal strip Replace thermal printhead assembly.
Impact Faint or light characters Dried out or worn fabric ink ribbon cartridge Replace fabric ink ribbon cartridge.
Impact Missing horizontal lines through characters Stuck or broken printhead solenoid pin Clean or replace dot-matrix printhead.

📏 M.2 Size Nomenclature (Width × Length)

  • 2242: 22 mm wide × 42 mm long (compact laptops and tablets).
  • 2230: 22 mm wide × 30 mm long (Steam Deck, handheld consoles).
  • 22110: 22 mm wide × 110 mm long (enterprise server SSDs with power-loss capacitors).

🧠 18. RAM Generations & Form Factors

Domain 3.0 Hardware

DDR generations, pin specifications, operating voltages, PMIC chips, and ECC error checking.

Generation Desktop DIMM Pins Laptop SO-DIMM Pins Operating Voltage Speed Range Architectural Distinctions
DDR3 240 pins 204 pins 1.5V (1.35V DDR3L) 800 – 2133 MT/s Single 64-bit channel per DIMM.
DDR4 288 pins 260 pins 1.2V (1.05V DDR4L) 1600 – 3200 MT/s Curved bottom edge to reduce insertion force. Key notch shifted off-center.
DDR5 288 pins 262 pins 1.1V 4800 – 8400+ MT/s Dual 32-bit sub-channels per stick; on-module Power Management IC (PMIC); on-die ECC. Notch differs from DDR4!
ECC vs. Non-ECC Memory: ECC (Error-Correcting Code) detects and automatically corrects single-bit errors in memory in real time, and halts on multi-bit errors. It features 9 memory chips per side instead of 8 (extra parity chip). Used in mission-critical enterprise servers and financial trading workstations. Requires motherboard and CPU ECC support (Intel Xeon, AMD EPYC/Threadripper).

🧰 19. Hardware Diagnostic Tools

Domain 3.0 Hardware & 5.0 Troubleshooting

Technician toolkit instrumentation: continuity testers, toner probes, OTDRs, multimeters, and PSU testers.

Diagnostic Tool Primary Measurement / Function CompTIA Exam Problem Scenario
Cable Tester (Continuity) Tests pin-to-pin electrical mapping and continuity on twisted pair copper cables. Identifies opens, shorts, crossed wires, reversed pairs, and split pairs in patch cables.
Toner Probe (Fox & Hound) Injects analog audio tone into wire; inductive probe detects tone without stripping jacket. Tracing an unmarked RJ-45 cable in a crowded wiring closet from wall jack to patch panel.
Loopback Plug Loops transmit (TX) pins directly back to receive (RX) pins. Testing whether a workstation NIC or switch port transceiver hardware is functional.
OTDR (Optical Time-Domain Reflectometer) Sends laser light pulses down fiber cable and measures backscatter reflections. Finding the precise distance in meters to a broken fiber optic cable, bend, or bad splice.
Optical Power Meter Measures optical light power attenuation in decibels (dB). Verifying whether fiber optic signal loss is within acceptable link budget thresholds.
Multimeter Measures AC/DC voltage, resistance (Ohms), and continuity (audible beep). Testing wall outlet AC voltage (~120V US / 230V EU) and PSU output rails (+12V, +5V, +3.3V).
Power Supply Tester Benchtop unit with 24-pin ATX, EPS, and SATA plugs with digital voltage readout. Testing a suspected dead PSU and measuring the Power Good (PG) signal delay (100-500 ms).
Wi-Fi / Spectrum Analyzer Measures 2.4/5/6 GHz RF signal strength (RSSI), channel overlap, and interference. Optimizing wireless AP channel placement and diagnosing dead zones or rogue access points.
Punchdown Tool Seats copper wires into 66/110 IDC blocks and trims excess wire ends simultaneously. Terminating Cat 6 cables onto a 110-block patch panel or RJ-45 wall keystone jack.
Crimper Compresses modular RJ-45 (8P8C) or RJ-11 connector onto cable end. Terminating a custom-length patch cable with a new plastic RJ-45 modular plug.
